title: Tarantino calls Hollywood a flavorless sausage factory and crowns Netflix thriller The Rip as his sole recent favorite
text:
In a blunt essay for Sight and Sound Magazine Quentin Tarantino denounces modern Hollywood for audience pandering and miscasting, yet praises the 2026 Netflix crime thriller The Rip as the only film in six years that fully captivated him.
Renowned filmmaker Quentin Tarantino has launched a scathing critique of contemporary Hollywood, describing the industry as a flavorless sausage factory that churns out movies driven by audience pandering and miscasting.
In a fiery essay for Sight and Sound Magazine the 63 year old director, a two time Oscar winner, confessed that watching modern cinema has become almost impossible for him. Despite his grim assessment he highlighted a single 2026 release that captured his full attention from start to finish: the Netflix crime thriller The Rip. Tarantino praised the film as an exhilarating cop drama built around a novel premise that delivers its thrills in clever and inventive ways.
He lauded the entire package including director Joe Carnahan, the screenplay, the splendid cast and the work of cinematographer Juan Miguel Azpiroz. The Rip stars Ben Affleck and Matt Damon in lead roles and features an ensemble that includes Sasha Calle, Teyana Taylor, Steven Yeun, Kyle Chandler, Scott Adkins and Catalina Sandino Moreno.
The story follows a group of Miami police officers who stumble upon a stash of millions in cash, sparking distrust as outsiders learn of the massive seizure and forcing the cops to question who they can rely on. The film debuted on Netflix in January and quickly earned positive reviews, posting a critics score of 77 percent on Rotten Tomatoes and an audience rating of 65 percent.
Tarantino's essay also mentioned other movies he has enjoyed in recent years such as the 2021 remake of West Side Story and Kevin Costner's Western saga Horizon an American Saga chapters one and two, which arrived in 2024. Nevertheless he noted that apart from The Rip few films in the past six years have managed to hold him in their grip and transport him to the magical realm of enjoyment that once defined his love of cinema.
He admitted that nowadays he would rather read a book than sit through most new releases. The director's criticism of Hollywood is not new. Late last year he attracted backlash after disparaging There Will Be Blood star Paul Dano, calling him weak and uninteresting during an appearance on the Bret Easton Ellis podcast. Celebrities such as Matthew Lillard, George Clooney and Daniel Day Lewis quickly defended Dano, and the actor later addressed the comments in an interview with Variety.
Tarantino also reiterated his admiration for Kevin Costner's recent westerns, emphasizing that well crafted storytelling and strong performances remain rare in today's production line. His essay paints a bleak picture of an industry that, in his view, has shifted from a source of artistic wonder to a vehicle for shallow profit, leaving audiences and creators alike yearning for the era when movies could still inspire genuine awe and emotional depth.
The Rip stands out as a surprising exception, offering a glimpse of what cinema can achieve when imagination, skillful direction and a cohesive ensemble come together in service of a compelling narrative
